decks.domain: Drugs, stopping, crashes and railroad crossings

cards.front: Which drugs can weaken your ability to drive safely?
cards.back: Many drugs can weaken your ability to drive safely, whether a doctor prescribed them or you bought them over the counter.

cards.front: What should you ask your doctor when taking prescription medicine?
cards.back: When you take prescription medicine, ask your doctor about any side effects that could affect your driving.

cards.front: Which ingredients in some cold and allergy pills can affect driving?
cards.back: Some non-prescription allergy remedies and cold pills contain codeine, alcohol, antihistamines or bromides, and each of these can affect driving.

cards.front: What side effects can antihistamines cause?
cards.back: Antihistamines, taken for cold congestion and allergies, can cause inattention, confusion and drowsiness, and some are even used as sleep aids.

cards.front: What are barbiturates, and what does overusing them do?
cards.back: Barbiturates are sedatives used mainly for sleep, and overusing them brings drowsiness, confusion and poor coordination much like drunkenness, leaving the person unfit to drive.

cards.front: How do the effects of antihistamines differ from overused barbiturates?
cards.back: Antihistamines may cause drowsiness and confusion as side effects, while barbiturates produce drunk-like symptoms when used to excess.

cards.front: What can the most dangerous illegal drugs do to a driver?
cards.back: The most dangerous drugs, such as LSD and heroin, are available only illegally and can leave users unaware of their surroundings, so no one under their influence may drive.

cards.front: What do studies cited in the manual say about marijuana and driving?
cards.back: Studies cited in the manual link marijuana use to more traffic-violation arrests, and experts agree it should not be used when driving.
cards.memory_hook: marijuana and driving do not mix

cards.front: What happens when alcohol is combined with drugs?
cards.back: Combining alcohol with drugs does not merely double the effect; it multiplies it and has caused deaths, so never drink while taking medicine.

cards.front: Who must tell a patient with a chronic illness about driving limits?
cards.back: For a chronic illness or physical impairment, the physician is responsible for telling the patient about any driving limits that may apply.

decks.module: Following distance and the two-second rule
decks.domain: Drugs, stopping, crashes and railroad crossings

cards.front: What causes most rear-end collisions, and which space can you control most easily?
cards.back: Following too closely causes most rear-end collisions, and the space ahead of your car, called following distance, is the space you can control most easily.

cards.front: What should decide your following distance?
cards.back: Set your following distance by the speed of traffic and the condition of the road, leaving enough room to stop if you must.
cards.memory_hook: speed and road set the gap

cards.front: Which rule replaced one car length for every ten miles per hour?
cards.back: The old rule of one car length for every ten miles per hour has given way to the two-second rule, which the manual calls easier to apply and safer.

cards.front: How do you use the two-second rule?
cards.back: For the two-second rule, pick a fixed object ahead, start counting one thousand one, one thousand two as the car ahead passes it, and if you reach it first, ease off until the gap is safe.

cards.front: When should you stretch the gap to four or five seconds?
cards.back: When road or weather conditions are poor, stretch the gap to a four- or five-second count, and use the longer gap too when driving a vehicle longer than a car.

cards.front: How does the following count change from good to poor conditions?
cards.back: The two-second count is for good conditions, while bad roads, bad weather or a long vehicle call for four or five seconds.
cards.memory_hook: two good, four or five bad

cards.front: What should you do when you see brake lights or a shrinking gap ahead?
cards.back: Watch for brake lights and a shrinking gap ahead, and move your foot to the brake pedal right away so you are ready to stop.

decks.domain: Drugs, stopping, crashes and railroad crossings

cards.front: What first decides actual stopping distance, and what does stopping distance help decide?
cards.back: How far your car needs to stop helps decide a safe speed, and actual stopping distance depends first on the driver's mental and physical reaction time.

cards.front: How does pavement affect stopping distance?
cards.back: Pavement type and condition change stopping distance a great deal, since rough dry concrete grips far better than slippery brick or smooth asphalt.

cards.front: Which tire factors determine your traction for stopping?
cards.back: Tire type, condition and tread depth all determine how much traction you have for stopping, so check the owner's manual or a dealer for the right tire size.

cards.front: How do wide tires and narrow tires differ in stopping?
cards.back: Large, wide tires may stop sooner on smooth dry roads but skid or hydroplane more easily when wet, while small, narrow tires may cut through standing water yet lose overall stopping power.
cards.memory_hook: wide grips dry, narrow cuts water

cards.front: Which car and brake factors affect stopping?
cards.back: Chassis design, weight distribution, suspension, shock absorbers and the type, condition and balance of the brakes all affect stopping, and a brake that locks before the others can cause serious trouble.

cards.front: How can wind affect a sudden stop at high speed?
cards.back: Wind direction and speed also affect stopping, and drivers often do not realize how much difference a strong tail wind makes during a sudden high-speed stop.

cards.front: What does the stopping chart show at twenty-five miles per hour?
cards.back: The manual's stopping-distance chart gives twenty-seven feet of thinking distance plus thirty-four point seven feet of braking distance, or sixty-one point seven feet in total, at twenty-five miles per hour

cards.front: What does the stopping chart show at fifty-five miles per hour?
cards.back: On the same chart, at fifty-five miles per hour a driver covers sixty feet while reacting and one hundred sixty-eight feet while braking, two hundred twenty-eight feet in all.

cards.front: What does the stopping chart show at sixty-five miles per hour?
cards.back: At sixty-five miles per hour the chart shows seventy-one feet of thinking distance and two hundred thirty-four point seven feet of braking distance, a total of three hundred five point seven feet.

decks.domain: Drugs, stopping, crashes and railroad crossings

cards.front: What must you do right away if you are in a crash?
cards.back: If you are in a crash you must stop at once and help anyone injured, call for medical help if needed, and warn other traffic with flags, flares or whatever you have before police arrive.

cards.front: When may you move an injured person after a crash?
cards.back: Do not move injured people unless it is absolutely necessary to get them away from fire or another danger, and keep them lying or sitting down until trained medical help arrives.

cards.front: What first aid should you give, and what warning does the manual add?
cards.back: Give first aid, keep the injured comfortable and treat for shock, but remember a layman can give too much first aid; a Red Cross or similar course is recommended.
cards.memory_hook: treat for shock, not too much

cards.front: What must you tell and show the others involved in any crash?
cards.back: In any type of crash you must stop, tell the others involved your name, address and registration number, and let them see your driver license.

cards.front: What information should you collect at a crash scene?
cards.back: At a crash, collect the names and addresses of everyone involved and of any witnesses, and note other relevant details.

cards.front: What must you give another person involved who asks about insurance?
cards.back: If another person involved asks, give the name and address of your liability insurance company and your local agent, and if you cannot do so at the scene, provide it later.

cards.front: What must you do if you hit an unattended vehicle?
cards.back: If you hit an unattended vehicle, either notify the police, try to find its owner, or leave a written note with your name and address where it will easily be seen on that vehicle.

cards.front: What must you do when a mishap damages other property?
cards.back: When a mishap damages any other kind of property, you must let the property owner know.

decks.module: Reporting crashes and the SR form
decks.domain: Drugs, stopping, crashes and railroad crossings

cards.front: Who must be told about a crash with injury or death, and how fast?
cards.back: A crash with injury or death must be reported by the fastest means available, to local police inside a city or town or to the State Troopers on a state highway.

cards.front: When is a written Form SR-thirty-one required, and how long do you have?
cards.back: After a crash with injury, death or five hundred dollars or more in damage, the involved driver has thirty days to send a written Form SR-thirty-one if the at-fault party was uninsured; when both parties were insured, neither files it.

cards.front: Where do SR-thirty-one forms go?
cards.back: SR-thirty-one forms go to the ALEA Safety Responsibility Unit by mail or can be submitted online through ALEA's driver license website.

cards.front: How does reporting an injury crash to police differ from the written SR form?
cards.back: A crash with injury or death is reported to police right away, while the written SR-thirty-one within thirty days applies when an uninsured at-fault party is involved.

cards.front: What should a witness include when reporting a crash?
cards.back: A witness reporting a crash should give the exact location, whether the road is blocked, and the likely damage and injuries, and every crash should go to the law enforcement agency with jurisdiction.

decks.domain: Drugs, stopping, crashes and railroad crossings (crash duties, railroads and confusables)

cards.front: What does the round railroad warning sign look like, and where does it stand?
cards.back: The round railroad warning sign is yellow with a black X and the letters RR, and it stands seven hundred fifty feet before the track to warn of a crossing ahead.

cards.front: What pavement markings may appear before a railroad crossing?
cards.back: Before a crossing the pavement may carry a large X with two R's, a yellow line ahead of it means no passing, and white lines beside the track mark where to stop for a train.

cards.front: What must you do when crossing lights start flashing?
cards.back: When crossing lights start flashing you must always stop and wait until it is safe to go.

cards.front: What must you do when crossing gates come down?
cards.back: Red flashing lights warn you to stop as crossing gates come down, and you stay stopped until the gates rise and the lights quit flashing.

cards.front: What should you do at a crossing with no warning device?
cards.back: At a crossing with no warning device, slow down and look and listen for trains before going on.

cards.front: What does the crossbuck sign mean, and what does a sign beneath it show?
cards.back: The crossbuck sign appears at most crossings and means slow down and be ready to stop when a train is seen; a sign under it shows the number of tracks when there is more than one.

cards.front: How does the advance railroad sign differ from the crossbuck?
cards.back: The advance railroad sign is round and yellow and stands seven hundred fifty feet before the track, while the crossbuck stands at the crossing itself.

cards.front: Which vehicles must stop before every railroad crossing?
cards.back: School buses, church buses, all passenger buses, and trucks hauling flammables, explosives or other hazardous material must stop before every railroad crossing.

cards.front: Within what distance of a railroad crossing must a stop be made?
cards.back: The manual says a stop at a railroad crossing must be made within fifteen to fifty feet of it.

cards.front: How fast should you approach a crossing, and when must you stop completely?
cards.back: Approach slowly enough to be sure you can stop once a train first comes into view, and come to a complete stop at crossings protected by electric or mechanical signals as the manual directs.

cards.front: When must you stop at a crossing, and what must you check with several tracks?
cards.back: You must stop when the crossing gate is down or a train is approaching, and with more than one track you must be sure every track is clear before crossing.

cards.front: When must buses and hazardous-material trucks stop at a crossing, and when must other drivers stop?
cards.back: Buses and hazardous-material trucks must always stop at crossings, while other drivers must stop for flashing lights, lowered gates or an approaching train.

decks.domain: Drugs, stopping, crashes and railroad crossings (crash duties, railroads and confusables)

cards.front: Why should you never change gears on the tracks?
cards.back: Never change gears while on the tracks, because that can stall the car; with a manual transmission, shift down before you cross.

cards.front: When should you expect a train, and what should you do in heavy traffic?
cards.back: Expect a train on any track at any hour, and in heavy traffic do not start across until you know you can clear the crossing.

cards.front: What should you watch for after the last car of a train passes?
cards.back: After the last car of a train passes, wait until you are sure no second train is coming on another track, especially from the opposite direction.

cards.front: Is it legal to drive around lowered gates or race a train?
cards.back: Driving around lowered gates is against the law, so stay put until they rise, and never race a train to the crossing.

cards.front: What should you be ready for when following buses or trucks near a crossing?
cards.back: Be ready to stop when you follow buses or trucks that are required to stop at crossings.

cards.front: What do crossing-crash statistics show about deaths and crossings with warning devices?
cards.back: Crossing crashes kill more people in the United States each year than all aviation crashes together, and nearly fifty percent of train-vehicle collisions happen at crossings with active warning devices.

cards.front: Where may you cross railroad tracks, and is walking on them allowed?
cards.back: Walking or playing on tracks, trestles, rail yards or equipment is illegal, and you should cross tracks only at designated crossings.

cards.front: What should you do if your vehicle stalls on a crossing?
cards.back: If your vehicle stalls on a crossing, get everyone out right away and clear of the tracks, then call local law enforcement for help.

cards.front: How far does a freight train at fifty-five miles per hour need to stop?
cards.back: Trains cannot stop quickly: a freight train going fifty-five miles per hour needs a mile or more, about the length of eighteen football fields.

recap_hooks.text: Ask about side effects, watch cold pill ingredients, never drive on illegal drugs, and never mix alcohol with medicine.

recaps.module: Following distance and the two-second rule

recap_hooks.text: Leave at least two seconds in good conditions and four or five when roads or weather are poor.
Reaction time, pavement, tires, brakes and wind all change stopping distance, and braking distance grows fast with speed.
After any crash, stop, help the injured without moving them unless necessary, and exchange your name, address, registration and license.

recaps.module: Reporting crashes and the SR form

recap_hooks.text: Report injury crashes to police right away, and send the written SR form within thirty days when an uninsured driver was at fault.
The round sign warns ahead, the crossbuck marks the crossing, and buses and hazardous-material trucks always stop.
Expect a train any time, watch for a second train, never go around gates, and get everyone out if you stall.

merges.justification: both are manual crossing-crash statistics taught together on the host card
